message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for me to tell my cousin that his kid can't stay in our house. Let me break this down step by step. First, my cousin moved in with my husband and me. We've made a separate flatlet for him, which is completely closed off from the main house. He has his own entrance, so it's like two separate units in one house. That seems pretty private and respectful of his space. Now, my cousin has a 2-year-old, and he's going through a custody battle with his ex. He wants to spend more time with his son, and I completely support that. I really hope he gets more time with his son because that's important for the child. Yesterday, my cousin asked if my husband and I could convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son. The thing is, there's no access from my cousin's room into our part of the house, and he doesn't have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court is looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son. Honestly, his current room and bathroom are more than big enough for the child. But here's the thing: I'm not comfortable letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him. I don't want to take responsibility for his kid, especially since there's no direct access between their space and ours. It feels like it could create a lot of issues, and I'm not sure if it's fair to the child or to us. The whole family is involved in this because that's just how my family is. Everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. But I'm wondering, would it be wrong for me to tell him I won't allow his son to stay in our house? Would that jeopardize his court case? On one hand, I want to support my cousin and help him get more time with his son. On the other hand, I have to consider my own comfort and the practical aspects of having his son in our house without him having easy access. It's a tough spot to be in. I guess I need to think about the potential consequences. If I say no, could that affect his custody case negatively? The court might see it as him not having a suitable space, even though his current setup is fine. But if I say yes, I'm taking on responsibility for his son without the convenience of him being able to come and go as needed. Is there a middle ground? Maybe I can suggest alternative arrangements or find a way to make the space accessible without compromising our own privacy. But I'm not sure if that's feasible. In the end, I have to weigh my support for my cousin against my own boundaries and the practicalities of the situation. It's a difficult decision, and I'm not entirely sure what the morally acceptable choice is here.
